title: One Family, United in Christ, By Different Languages
excerpt: At Holy Rosary's Parish Feast and Cultural Day, many Nigerian languages, traditions, songs, and foods come together in the shared life of Christ.
body:
I grew up in a world connected by technology, but even with the whole globe at my fingertips, I still saw the hate between cultures online. Every comment section seemed to pull people further into their own corners. We had the tools to understand one another better than any generation before us, yet what I saw most often was division and suspicion toward anyone who spoke differently.

That is why stepping into Holy Rosary Parish, Wuse, Abuja for our Parish Feast/Cultural Day has always felt like discovering another world entirely. Our Feast Day is now a true Cultural Display.

I remember growing up watching my mom and her dance partner, **Miss Tope**. What always struck me was that Miss Tope never thought of my mom as "just another Igbo woman." She never saw that line. To Miss Tope, my mom was simply a mom who didn't speak her mother tongue, but who enjoyed music just as much as she did. When the drums start, they will grab each other's hands and dance, laughing, completely in sync. Miss Tope didn't see two cultures meeting; she just saw a mom in God's house. That was my first lesson that the church does not see tribe.

## The Sanctuary Became a Village Square

Where the online world draws battle lines, our parish built a table.

This year, the heart of it all was again the music. Our choir gave a devoted effort that words can hardly capture. Months of learning and rehearsing songs from across Nigeria - Igbo highlife praise, Yoruba *oriki*, Hausa soulful chants, Efik, and Ibibio hymns, Tiv rhythms - blending them all into one liturgy.

When they sang, you heard not just harmony, but sacrifice and a deep respect for every culture in the pews.

## When Parts of the Mass Were Spoken in Our Mother Tongues

It sounded like the Mass was finally home for everyone.

During the Prayers of the Faithful, intentions were lifted, not just in English, but in **Igbo, Yoruba, Hausa, Ibibio, Idoma, Igala and other dialects** - the languages and dialects our parents use to pray at home. Parts of the Mass were echoed in our native tongues. At that moment, it was Pentecost again. God didn't erase our languages to make us one; He used them to build a bridge.

The beauty of our various Nigerian cultures was everywhere to see. The sanctuary was a rainbow of **Aso-Oke, George wrappers, Isiagu, Ankara, and flowing Babariga**. Red caps, coral beads, hand-woven akwete, gele tied in grand styles - each colour told the story of a people, yet together they painted one beautiful portrait of Christ's Body.

Then came the aroma. After Mass, the air was filled with the smell of different cultures' food - the peppery warmth of **ofe nsala, amala and ewedu, smoky suya, rich afang and edikang ikong, tuwo and soups from the North** - all shared freely from the same table. We didn't just see our diversity; we tasted it.

And if you were here last year (2025), you will never forget **Fr. Kale's dance steps** during the cultural celebration. The way Father danced - with so much joy and freedom, moving from Igbo steps to Yoruba steps without missing a beat - was his own homily. It was his appreciation for the bond we have, irrespective of culture. He showed us that leadership in this family means dancing with everyone. No one was left on the side.

## We Are a Family

The online world taught me how easy it is for humans to divide. But our Feast/Cultural Day has shown me how powerful Christ is in bringing us together.

My mom and Miss Tope taught me as a child, and Fr. Kale reminded us last year that, in this parish, we are not Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Tiv, Igala, Nupe, or Efik first. Rather, we are family first.

Our different languages, our colours, our foods, and our songs do not push us apart. They simply give us a thousand more beautiful ways to say what we have always known here: *You belong here. Welcome home.*

**Happy Feast/Cultural Day**
